what: call and return nodes in the ICFG dump have no source line numbers
why: the ICFG toString printed only the raw LLVM instruction; the source-location helper was private to PAG.cpp
how: move value2String to SVFUtil and use it in the ICFG node toString methods

what: incomplete call graph construction caused by insufficient modeling of Java thread execution and library behavior Incomplete call graph construction for Java threads and lambda-based Runnable objects, with missing calls to Runnable.run() and PrintStream.println()
why: The thread analysis relied on imprecise abstract interpretation rather than the selected call graph algorithm's type information, causing missing Runnable.run() edges.
how: Updated the thread analysis to use the call graph algorithm's type iterator for resolving Runnable targets

what: Ensure sound Mod/Ref analysis for external functions whose memory side effects are not explicitly modeled, without unnecessarily sacrificing analysis precision.
why: SVF interpreted missing side-effect information as the absence of memory accesses, causing getModRefInfo() to incorrectly return NoModRef for unmodeled external calls
how: Conservatively return ModRef for external calls without recorded side effects. The maintainer instead favored explicitly specifying library side effects through ExtAPI to improve precision. The PR was closed without merging.

what: Preventing leak-analysis crashes when encountering nonstandard allocation function declarations.
why: The leak checker identified allocation functions by name and assumed their return values were pointers represented in the pointer-only SVFG. An integer-returning malloc violated this assumption, triggering an assertion failure.
how: Added return-type validation to skip non-pointer allocation results and introduced an option to construct a full SVFG for broader value-flow analysis.

what: Ensuring that dynamically added external-function summaries remain compatible with changes to the specification format.
why: A specification format update introduced return and argument type fields, but the runtime entry-creation API was not updated, producing incomplete and incompatible entries.
how: Extended the API to include the required function signatures, improved error reporting, and added helpers for managing function-overwrite settings.

what: Simplifying and improving the maintainability and expressiveness of external-function modeling in SVF, particularly for functions with complex memory behaviors.
why: undetermined
how: Replaced ExtAPI.json with annotated C stubs in extapi.c, compiled into LLVM bitcode (extapi.bc) and loaded alongside the application. Updated SVF's external-call handling to interpret the annotations and model memory behavior.

what: Supporting precise and expressive external-function summaries, including allocation wrappers with complex pointer operations, while maintaining consistent allocation and aliasing semantics.
why: The redesigned extapi.c format could not combine per-call-site allocation semantics with explicit memory operations, and migration from ExtAPI.json introduced contradictory allocation annotations.
how: Removed the conflicting STATIC annotation and rewrote affected library models to represent static allocations explicitly. More comprehensive support for complex allocation wrappers was proposed but remained unresolved.

what: Handling GEP statements generated during external-function modeling without causing invalid memory accesses when computing byte offsets.
why: AccessPath::computeConstantByteOffset() assumed all GEP offset entries contained valid type information, but GEP statements generated for memcpy-like external calls omitted this information (nullptr), violating that assumption.
how: Added an explicit assertion and documentation explaining that computeConstantByteOffset() does not support external API-generated GEP statements. The fix does not enable byte-offset computation for these GEPs; it only detects unsupported usage and provides a clearer diagnostic instead of a null-pointer dereference.

what: Ensuring consistent points-to analysis results across different module-loading APIs, including support for external-library function modeling.
why: The external API loading function, loadExtAPIModules(), was invoked only by the file-based buildSVFModule() overload. The in-memory overload omitted this initialization step, causing external functions to be analyzed without their summaries.
how: PR #1258 updated buildSVFModule(Module&) to load extapi.bc using the application's LLVMContext, ensuring external-function models are available for in-memory modules.

topic: Modeling entry points and program initialization
what: Supporting call graph construction for Android applications that lack conventional main() entry points.
why: undetermined
how: Added Android-specific entry-point discovery using manifest-declared launcher activities and lifecycle methods. ICC modeling remained future work.

topic: Modeling entry points and program initialization
what: Ensuring complete and consistent call graph construction across different algorithms by accounting for implicit JVM startup behavior and native library initialization.
why: OPAL's models of JVM initialization were incomplete and inconsistent. JDK 11+ initialization methods were missing from configured entry points, native initialization effects were not properly represented, and some algorithms used incompatible mechanisms for tracking instantiated types.
how: Expanded JVM initialization and native-method configurations, preserved entry points without method bodies, and corrected instantiated-type propagation for XTA.

topic: Modeling entry points and program initialization
what: Preserving interprocedural value-flow dependencies involving C++ global objects initialized before main().
why: SVF did not automatically include runtime-invoked global constructor functions in the call graph rooted at main(). These functions are registered through llvm.global_ctors, making initialization stores invisible to downstream value-flow analysis unless explicitly modeled.
how: Used the artificial svf.main entry point to model global initialization and improved its construction to identify global constructors and destructors through LLVM metadata rather than function-name heuristics.

topic: Modeling entry points and program initialization
what: Ensuring that all analyses consistently recognize the artificial svf.main entry point so global initialization effects are included in flow-sensitive pointer analysis.
why: Although -svf-main constructed an artificial entry point for global constructors, multiple analysis components still hard-coded main as the entry function. This caused analyses to bypass global initialization and miss function-pointer assignments.
how: Centralized entry-point recognition to support svf.main consistently across analyses and adjusted the option when no artificial entry point exists.

what: Preserving correct operand-stack semantics when translating stack-based Java bytecode into variable-based three-address code.
why: The TAC generator assumed variable IDs always corresponded to operand-stack positions, but instructions such as dup did not maintain this invariant. As a result, return instructions incorrectly referenced a fixed variable ID.
how: Updated return-instruction generation to use the actual top-of-stack variable (stack.head) instead of a predefined variable with ID 0. This corrected return-value handling without changing the underlying variable-renumbering mechanism.

what: Maintaining correct and robust LLVM IR preprocessing as LLVM's instruction representation and API requirements evolve.
why: SVF's custom constant-expression conversion relied on LLVM accepting a null source element type when constructing GEP instructions. LLVM 13 no longer supported this assumption, causing a segmentation fault
how: replaced the hand-written constant-expression conversion logic with LLVM's ConstantExpr::getAsInstruction() API, allowing LLVM to construct the corresponding instruction with the appropriate type information

what: Only loads globals from one module and hence an assert fails when loading globals for other module. Assumption is not clearly communication between components
why: fix to load globals from all .ll files
how: modified both addGlobalValueMap() and getSVFGlobalValue() to normalize globals to their representative values before insertion and lookup, ensuring consistent mapping to SVFGlobalValue

what: Ensuring robust PAG construction while maintaining consistency between graph edges and their associated function contexts.
why: Undetermined. An older SVF revision triggered a function-membership assertion during PAG construction, but the issue discussion provides no diagnosis of the underlying defect.
how: undetermined

what: Supporting uncommon or newly encountered LLVM IR constructs during PAG/VFG construction without incorrectly requiring definitions for values that do not have them.
why: SVF did not recognize MetadataAsValue as constant data. Consequently, the VFG expected a definition for a metadata argument passed to an LLVM intrinsic, triggering an assertion failure.
how: Commit 2dd0181 updated PAGNode::isConstantData() to recognize MetadataAsValue as constant data, so these nodes no longer require ordinary value definitions.

what: Ensuring complete instruction coverage when translating LLVM IR operations into PAG edges, so downstream value-flow graphs have the required definitions.
why: The PAG builder lacked handlers for LLVM's va_arg and freeze instructions. As a result, their output values had no defining PAG statements, causing an assertion failure during SVFG construction
how: Commit 04a0691 added PAGBuilder::visitVAArgInst() and visitFreezeInst(), representing these instructions with copy edges from their operands to their results. It also added empty visitors for va_start, va_end, and va_copy.

what: Reliably constructing program value-flow graphs from LLVM bitcode generated by different language front ends, such as Rust, while distinguishing analysis defects from malformed inputs or environment-specific failures.
why: undetermined
how: No code change. The maintainer reported that the assertion did not reproduce and advised that the other failure was related to input bitcode generation.

what: Missing edges in SVFG
why: SVF's SVFG is primarily designed to track pointer-related value flows for pointer analysis and memory error detection. Although allocation sizes and GEP indices can affect memory safety and address calculations, their values do not directly determine the pointer targets modeled by the SVFG's points-to analysis. Consequently, SVF intentionally omitted these non-pointer def-use relationships.
how: No fix was implemented. The maintainer acknowledged the limitation

what: Constructing program graphs at the appropriate abstraction level while avoiding redundant instructions and unnecessary dependencies on other graph representations.
why: CFBasicBlockG was built indirectly by traversing ICFG nodes rather than the underlying SVFBasicBlock structures, and the builder did not filter redundant intrinsic instructions.
how: Reworked CFBasicBlockGBuilder to iterate directly over functions and basic blocks in the SVF module, while still using ICFG nodes to represent relevant instructions and call/return boundaries. Added filtering through SVFUtil::isIntrinsicInst() to exclude unnecessary intrinsic instructions.

what: Preserving control-flow and path-condition information when simplifying value-flow graphs, so downstream analyses can correctly distinguish feasible execution paths.
why: SaberSVFGBuilder removed indirect value-flow edges during strong updates, but ProgSlice did not account for these removed edges when computing value-flow guards. Consequently, a conditional value-flow relationship was incorrectly treated as unconditional.
how: recorded the edges removed by strong updates and incorporated their associated branch conditions into value-flow guard computation, excluding infeasible paths. The PR also separated the CFL and Saber SVFG builders to accommodate their different requirements.

what: Correctly representing value flows through aggregate operations, particularly structures returned by value, to support accurate memory-error detection.
why: SVF did not model returning a local struct by value, which LLVM IR expresses through extractvalue/insertvalue unpacking of the aggregate. The struct's value was therefore not copied to the caller, and the two frees of the same buffer were not connected in the value-flow graph.
how: No implementation fix. The maintainer acknowledged the limitation and suggested inlining the local-variable return as a workaround, with which Saber reports the double free correctly.

what: OPAL to classify valid bytecode as unreachable and fail while regenerating the StackMapTable
why: undetermined
how: undetermined

topic: Modeling reflection and dynamic language features
what: Supporting evolving Java reflection APIs while preserving correct abstract interpretation of dynamically resolved class objects.
why: OPAL's reflection model explicitly recognized only older Class.forName() signatures. New JDK overloads were not handled, and the module-based overloads also had different semantics that required additional consideration.
how: The issue was addressed through multiple PRs: - OPAL-97: Added support for newer private Class.forName() overloads, resolving the original DomainException. - OPAL-152: Added handling for module-based overloads using a conservative approximation that returns the named class without tracking module restrictions. - OPAL-153: Updated the associated integration-test reference files.

what: Robustly constructing class hierarchy graphs when constructors contain indirect calls whose targets cannot be statically resolved.
why: The CHG builder assumed all constructor call sites had known callees and dereferenced the result of getCallee() without checking for nullptr, causing a segmentation fault on indirect calls.
how: Commit e6c4fedb added a defensive null-callee check to skip unresolved indirect call sites during inheritance-edge construction.

what: Accurately distinguishing base-class initialization from member-object initialization when inferring C++ inheritance relationships from LLVM IR.
why: The constructor-based inheritance heuristic lacked an effective check for distinguishing base-class and member-object constructor calls. The disabled this-pointer comparison caused SVF to incorrectly interpret member-object initialization as inheritance.
how: SVF-1539 remains open, with no directly linked fix. However, the later PR SVF-1774 rewrote and re-enabled isSameThisPtrInConstructor() for opaque-pointer LLVM IR and distinguished base-class GEP patterns from member-field GEP patterns. This addressed the same underlying false-inheritance mechanism, although SVF-1774 formally references SVF-1773 rather than SVF-1539

what: Maintaining accurate C++ inheritance inference when changes to LLVM IR invalidate existing constructor-pointer identification heuristics.
why: LLVM 15+ opaque pointers removed the bitcast pattern used by isSameThisPtrInConstructor(). The check was subsequently disabled, allowing member-object constructor calls to be misclassified as inheritance. The existing helper also mishandled constructors with sret parameters.
how: Rewrote isSameThisPtrInConstructor() to support opaque-pointer IR patterns and distinguish base-class initialization from member-field initialization. Restored the check in CHG construction and updated getConstructorThisPtr() to handle sret parameters.

what: Robustly handling constructor/destructor functions with unexpected or missing arguments during class hierarchy inference.
why: CHGBuilder::connectInheritEdgeViaCall() assumed constructor/destructor callers always contained arguments and invoked getConstructorThisPtr() without validating that assumption. This triggered an assertion for a zero-argument destructor.
how: Added an early return when caller->arg_size() == 0, preventing invalid argument access.

what: Precisely representing interprocedural memory side effects involving global pointers while balancing context sensitivity and analysis scalability.
why: SVF's interprocedural Mod-Ref analysis promotes global objects and their reachable pointees as side effects of call sites in a context-insensitive manner. Consequently, the SVFG may contain spurious value-flow paths between distinct calls to the same function.
how: No implementation fix was provided. The maintainer suggested implementing a context-sensitive Mod-Ref analysis or refining the SVFG after construction to eliminate spurious value flows. Both approaches would require additional analysis mechanisms.

what: Correctly mapping nested aggregate fields to their flattened memory representations when constructing points-to graphs.
why: The PAG builder mixed two indexing schemes: local field indices within nested structs and flattened offsets within the outer aggregate. Consequently, it retrieved incorrect field types and constructed incorrect GEP representations. A separate regression in GEP-node mapping caused multiple initializer stores to share the same field node.
how: The developer changed global-initializer handling to use the accumulated flattened field offset instead of the inner structure's field index.

what: Correctly handling synthetic and derived memory objects whose representations differ from ordinary allocation-site objects.
why: ContextDDA::isHeapCondMemObj() assumed that all heap objects had a valid LLVM allocation instruction as their reference value. However, SVF also classified dummy objects and their derived GEP objects as heap objects despite their missing refVal, causing null-pointer assertions.

what: Correctly managing ownership and lifetime of intermediate analysis objects that are created during one analysis phase and reused by subsequent phases.
why: MRVer objects were allocated during MemSSA construction and remained referenced during SVFG construction, but their ownership and destruction were not properly managed. Removing them from MemSSA's internal stacks did not release their memory, while destroying them immediately after MemSSA construction invalidated references used by SVFG.
how: No directly linked implementation fix was recorded in the issue. The maintainer suggested releasing the memory-region versions after SVFG construction, potentially through clearMSSA().

what: Recovering underlying aggregate types from LLVM IR when generic pointers, casts, and loads obscure the type information required for precise memory-operation modeling.
why: SVFIRBuilder::getBaseValueForExtArg() handled only limited patterns when tracing external-call arguments to their underlying typed objects. It could not recover struct types from an allocation whose typed representation appeared in a later cast or from a load through a bitcast pointer.
how: Extended type recovery to recognize these additional IR patterns. For heap-allocation results, SVF searches for a unique cast user that reveals the intended type. For loads through bitcast pointers, it traces back to the original pointer operand to recover type information.

what: Accurately resolving struct fields when low-level pointer arithmetic uses negative byte offsets that do not directly correspond to the field indices used by the memory model.
why: SVF's field-sensitive memory model represents aggregate fields using flattened indices but lacks the necessary mapping from negative byte offsets to the corresponding fields. Consequently, negative-offset GEP operations can produce incorrect points-to relationships.
how: Unresolved. The maintainer acknowledged the limitation and invited a contribution.

what: Supporting safe, node-specific modifications to points-to sets when their underlying representations are shared for memory efficiency.
why: SVF's default -ptd=persistent configuration allows nodes with identical points-to sets to share the same underlying data structure. Directly mutating a shared set therefore affects other nodes referencing that set.
how: The maintainer recommended using -ptd=mutable, which gives each node an independent points-to set representation and avoids unintended changes to other nodes. No source-code modification was required.

what: Accurately modeling individual array elements and their relationships with overlapping struct fields in field-sensitive pointer analysis.
why: Andersen's analysis models arrays field-insensitively by default, collapsing accesses to distinct array elements into a shared abstract field. This loses the distinction between function pointers stored in different elements of a union's array representation. The reason -model-arrays failed to change the result remains undetermined.
how: Unresolved. The maintainer acknowledged the limitation and invited a contribution.

what: Reliably resolving indirect calls involving pointer arithmetic across different compiler-generated LLVM IR representations.
why: Undetermined The reported indirect-call edge was missing in the x86-generated IR analysis but appeared in the ARM-generated IR analysis. The discussion did not identify why the results differed.
how: No code fix was implemented.

what: Maintaining consistent class identity information between class hierarchy construction and virtual-call target resolution.
why: SVF inconsistently normalized C++ class names: CHG construction preserved namespace qualifications, but virtual-call resolution removed them when extracting class names from demangled constructor names. This caused class hierarchy lookups to fail and omitted valid virtual-call edges.
how: Removed the unnecessary namespace-stripping operation in cppUtil::extractClsNamesFromFunc(), allowing class names used during virtual-call resolution to match those stored in the CHG.

what: Coordinating indirect thread-call resolution with pointer analysis so newly discovered call graph edges can contribute additional pointer constraints during analysis.
why: Indirect thread-creation targets were resolved in a post-processing phase, after pointer analysis had finished. Consequently, newly discovered fork edges and their argument-to-parameter relationships did not feed back into constraint solving. This phase-ordering problem is inferred from the patch rather than explicitly diagnosed in the PR description.
how: Extended on-the-fly call graph resolution to discover indirect fork targets during Andersen and Steensgaard pointer analysis, add the corresponding thread-call edges, and connect actual arguments to formal parameters

what: Maintaining accurate indirect-call resolution when LLVM IR represents equivalent aggregate types through different type identities and pointer casts.
why: undetermined
how: No implementation fix. The maintainer explained that SVF had migrated to LLVM 16 and did not intend to maintain both typed-pointer and opaque-pointer configurations. The reporter was asked whether the problem also occurred with opaque pointers, but no follow-up result was recorded.

what: Preserving the structural integrity and slot ordering of virtual function tables when compiler-generated thunks cannot be resolved to their underlying functions.
why: CHGBuilder::addFuncToFuncVector() assumed thunk targets could be resolved and omitted an entry when getThunkTarget() returned nullptr. Consequently, subsequent vtable entries shifted, causing incorrect virtual-call target resolution.
how: When the underlying target cannot be resolved, retain the thunk function itself as a placeholder rather than omitting the entry. This preserves the original vtable slot ordering.

topic: Correctness and precision of client analyses
what: Ensuring sound and scheduling-independent client-analysis results when combining information from dependent analyses.
why: The L3 string analysis conditionally introduced a null alternative based on whether its field-access dependency was interim or final. Consequently, different analysis schedules could produce different string-value approximations for the same program
how: Modified L3FieldReadInterpreter to always include null as a possible value for reference-typed fields, removing the dependency on field-access analysis completion. A special case preserves precise constant values for suitable static final fields outside high-soundness mode. The associated tests were updated. The fix deliberately accepts some loss of precision to obtain a more conservative, scheduling-independent result.

topic: Correctness and precision of client analyses
what: Accurately distinguishing object initialization from subsequent mutation, including assignments performed outside constructors on newly created, non-escaped objects.
why: OPAL's field mutability analysis treated initialization as occurring only inside constructors. As a result, it classified fields initialized through patterns such as copy() or clone() as mutable, reducing analysis precision.
how: Unspecified

topic: Correctness and precision of client analyses
what: IFDSLinearConstantAnalysis was not implemented
why: IFDSLinearConstantAnalysis was an unfinished demonstration analysis whose flow functions were left as identity functions. It therefore did not implement the transfer semantics required for linear constant propagation.
how: No implementation fix was made.

topic: Correctness and precision of client analyses
what: Accurately propagating taint through structured data and interprocedural argument passing in client analyses.
why: Undetermined. The ifds-taint analysis failed to detect taint flowing through a struct field into a by-value function argument, but the issue discussion did not identify the failing transfer function or establish whether bitcast handling was responsible.
how: No implementation fix was provided. The maintainer recommended using the existing IDEExtendedTaintAnalysis, described as more precise and robust, with improved parametrization. The reporter did not confirm whether this alternative resolved the example.

topic: Correctness and precision of client analyses
what: Precisely tracking initialization states of individual aggregate fields in data-flow analyses, particularly for compiler-generated field-by-field initialization patterns.
why: The existing IFDS uninitialized-variable analysis represents data-flow facts at the whole-value level and cannot distinguish initialized from uninitialized indices within an aggregate. This coarse abstraction incorrectly treats partially initialized aggregate values as wholly uninitialized.
how: Introduce an index-aware uninitialized-variable analysis using IndexWrapper<llvm::Value>, which combines an LLVM value with a sequence of aggregate indices. The proposed analysis handles InsertValueInst and ExtractValueInst at the appropriate indices, allowing it to track field initialization individually. The PR is open and not merged according to the supplied record. Therefore, this should be recorded as a proposed implementation, not a completed fix.

topic: Correctness and precision of client analyses
what: Accurately distinguishing and reporting branch-specific execution conditions in path-sensitive client analyses.
why: Saber's existing CUDD-based path-condition infrastructure did not distinguish true and false branches in the reported leak warnings, causing different conditional memory-freeing behaviors to produce identical messages.
how: The maintainer stated that Saber was transitioning from CUDD to Z3 to support more precise path-condition handling.

topic: Correctness and precision of client analyses
what: correctly identifying branch directions when reporting path-sensitive analysis results
why: Saber's BDD-based condition manager did not properly implement negated-condition recognition: isNegCond() always returned false, and negated conditions were not registered in the condition map. Consequently, conditional free paths were incorrectly reported as True branches.
how: Will replace BDD with Z3

topic: Correctness and precision of client analyses
what: Accurately computing path-sensitive value-flow conditions when strong-update optimizations remove graph edges that encode conditional overwrites.
why: Strong-update edge pruning and downstream path-condition computation made inconsistent assumptions. The graph builder removed an indirect value-flow edge representing an overwrite, but ProgSlice did not account for the removed edge and treated the surviving value flow as unconditional.
how: Final correction in SVF-1309: Instead of inferring the alternative branch from the remaining graph, the revised implementation explicitly recorded edges removed by strong updates and used their branch conditions to constrain surviving value flows.

topic: Correctness and precision of client analyses
what: Robustly evaluating path conditions across different LLVM IR branch representations, including constant-valued branch conditions.
why: SaberCondAllocator::evaluateTestNullLikeExpr() assumed conditional branches were controlled by variables with corresponding graph nodes. When encountering a constant branch condition, it attempted to cast a null graph node, triggering an assertion.
how: PR SVF-1594 added a check for constant branch conditions and returns Condition::nullExpr() rather than attempting to interpret them as variable-based null comparisons. The reporter confirmed that the fix resolved the crash.

what: Ensuring that an analysis framework correctly schedules interdependent analyses by accounting for both directly consumed properties and dependencies introduced by reusable analysis components.
why: Several FPCF analysis schedulers manually declared incomplete uses sets. In addition, dependencies introduced by their shared TypeIterator components were not propagated to the scheduler. Consequently, the framework could construct execution orders that failed to satisfy analyses' actual property requirements.
how: Added missing direct property dependencies and updated schedulers to include the property kinds used by their configured TypeIterator, using usedPropertyKinds. These changes covered multiple call-graph, points-to, reflection, and taint-analysis schedulers.

what: Correctly initializing and propagating data-flow facts across solver phases while respecting the lattice semantics used to encode IFDS analyses.
why: IDESolver did not report IFDS results at certain call sites and wrongly assigned BOTTOM instead of TOP
how: changed IFDS seed initialization from TOP to BOTTOM, allowing seeded facts to propagate correctly.

what: Enabling users to reconstruct and inspect data-flow propagation paths while balancing the memory and computational overhead of retaining provenance information.
why: The existing IFDS/IDE solver retained computed facts but did not record the explicit propagation edges needed for witness-path reconstruction. Maintaining a complete ESG could be prohibitively expensive, so this capability had not been implemented.
how: Introduced an opt-in path-tracing infrastructure consisting of three major components: - PathAwareIDESolver: Extends the IDE solver to record data-flow propagation edges through a new saveEdges hook. - ExplodedSuperGraph and PathSensitivityManager: Store propagation relationships and reconstruct the paths reaching a queried program point and fact. - Z3BasedPathSensitivityManager: Uses branch conditions encoded as Z3 constraints to filter infeasible propagation paths. The implementation also avoids recording some redundant intra-basic-block identity flows to reduce the size of the stored graph.

what: Designing flexible data-flow analysis APIs that allow alternative implementations of edge-function composition and joining without requiring redundant methods.
why: The IsEdgeFunction type trait unconditionally required compose() and join(), even when the analysis implemented these operations elsewhere. Because extend() and combine() are virtual methods, the existing framework could not determine at compile time whether they were overridden.
how: Made compose() and join() optional by introducing HasEFCompose and HasEFJoin traits. The framework now uses descriptive runtime errors when neither the edge function nor the analysis provides the required operation. Redundant placeholder implementations were removed

what: Maintaining correct and precise field-sensitive data-flow semantics while controlling the computational and memory overhead of access-path representations and edge-function operations.
why: The CFL-based field-sensitive analysis contained several implementation limitations: access-path equality ignored field offsets, edge-function combination was not monotone, alias handling was incomplete for some clients, and uncached edge functions and large kill-sets introduced performance overhead. These causes are derived primarily from the PR commits rather than an explicit root-cause discussion.
how: The PR made several related improvements: - Corrected analysis semantics: Included offsets in AccessPath equality and fixed the monotonicity of combine(). - Improved alias handling: Extended support for strong updates and analyses that do not generate all aliases. - Reduced representation overhead: Compressed and interned kill-sets using SmallArraySet, making access paths smaller and cheaper to copy. - Optimized edge-function computation: Interned edge functions and cached composition and join results, enabling constant-time comparisons of interned functions. - Improved instrumentation: Replaced ad hoc performance instrumentation with PAMM.

what: Correctly implementing abstract-domain operators and execution-state operations to preserve the mathematical properties required for sound and convergent abstract interpretation.
why: SVF's interval abstract domain contained several algorithmic implementation errors, including incorrect bound comparisons in widening, incorrect narrowing updates, reversed widening operands, an invalid iterator comparison during joining, and incomplete bottom-state checks that ignored abstract memory-location values. These causes are inferred from the patch rather than explicitly explained in the PR discussion.
how: Corrected the widening and narrowing implementations, repaired state joining and comparison logic, ensured widening operated on the intended receiver state, and extended bottom-state checking to account for memory-location values.

what: Analysis performance improvement
why: Undeterminded
how: Replaced recursive WTO-component traversal with a FIFO worklist over ICFG nodes through handleFunction(), while retaining WTO-based cycle detection and widening/narrowing in handleCycleWTO().

what: Preserving complete abstract-state semantics when replacing dense control-flow-based propagation with sparse value-flow-based propagation.
why: The full-sparse interpreter implicitly depended on dense ICFG propagation for branch-refined values and freed-address information. These state components were not fully represented in the SVFG, so disabling joinStates() caused the corresponding information to be lost.
how: Unresolved in this PR. After several design pivots, the PR was closed and the work continued in SVF-1821 by the same author.

what: Designing scalable sparse abstract interpretation that preserves path feasibility, memory-update semantics, and sufficient precision while reducing the overhead of dense state propagation.
why: Dense and semi-sparse execution maintained abstract object values across numerous ICFG nodes, increasing memory consumption. However, indirect SVFG edges alone were insufficient for replacing this mechanism because they did not encode all branch-feasibility and intervening-store information required to determine which abstract values could reach a use.
how: Implemented a full-sparse mode that pulls object values along indirect SVFG edges only when a branch-feasible ICFG path exists and no intermediate store redefines the same object. Branch feasibility was separated from branch refinement, and GepObjVar values fall back to dense joinStates. Benchmarks showed lower peak memory than the semi-sparse mode.

what: Maintaining a coherent and extensible abstract-state architecture while avoiding redundant or overlapping numerical-domain implementations.
why: Undertermined
how: Consolidate all domains into one: BoxProgramState But commits not merged.

what: The analysis never terminates
why: Undetermined
how: Unresolved

what: Improving static-analysis performance through efficient data structures while preserving the behavioral assumptions and result consistency of dependent analysis components.
why: The existing std::map incurred overhead in frequently accessed points-to data. However, replacing containers exposed dependencies on deterministic iteration, iterator stability, and custom hashing/equality behavior across SVF.
how: STL-based implementation

what: Efficiently maintaining pointer-analysis results when dynamically discovered call-graph edges introduce new value-flow dependencies.
why: When an on-the-fly call graph update added an indirect edge, updateConnectedNodes propagated the yielded version to every version relying on it rather than only to the newly connected consumed version. With over 200k new edges on some benchmarks, this all-or-nothing propagation caused massive redundant work; reliance sets stored as Set<Version> added further overhead.
how: Added a propagateVersion overload that propagates a version to one specific target version and used it in updateConnectedNodes. The version reliance map was changed from Set<Version> to std::vector<Version>.

what: Scaling expensive pre-analysis phases of flow-sensitive pointer analysis to very large programs without excessive time or memory consumption.
why: the versioning phase of SVF's versioned flow-sensitive analysis is a costly pre-analysis step
how: Parallelized meld labeling with worker threads that process prelabeled objects from a shared queue, configurable via a new -versioning-threads option, and replaced map-based caches with arrays. The PR was closed on the same day after review, with an assertion for the opt-svfg restriction agreed upon.

what: Running whole-program pointer analyses on large real-world programs within available memory.
why: Undetermined. The maintainer explained that std::bad_alloc means the process ran out of memory but did not identify which analysis data structure grows or why.
how: No code change. The maintainer could not reproduce a crash, and the issue was closed without further diagnosis.

what: Balancing analysis soundness and scalability as framework improvements make analyses more conservative on large C++ programs.
why: SVF had improved its soundness for C++ programs, so Andersen's analysis resolves and analyzes many more indirect call targets on STL- and virtual-call-heavy programs such as xalancbmk. This cost is not controlled by the field- and context-sensitivity options the user tried.
how: No code change. The maintainer suggested limiting resolved indirect call targets with -ind-call-limit and trying the Simplified-STL side project to reduce STL analysis overhead. The issue remains open.

what: Producing deterministic and reproducible analysis results across repeated runs on the same program and configuration.
why: Non-determinism is expected by design: the Soot-based fact generation depends on the order in which classes are found, and some reflection-analysis algorithms are randomized when electing representatives of class equivalence classes.
how: No code change. The maintainer recommended generating the facts once (--facts-only) and reusing them in later runs (--input-id), which removes the main source of non-determinism, although some reflection settings may still introduce variation.

what: Constructing a consistent class hierarchy and call graph when the input class path contains conflicting duplicate class files.
why: eclipse.jar bundles several conflicting class files for the same class. OPAL keeps the first one it parses, so the class hierarchy, and with it the call graph, depends on which nested jar is parsed first, which varies between runs.
how: Won't fix. The maintainer declared it expected behavior, pointing to the existing duplicate-class warning, since multiple conflicting class files on the class path are considered a user error. An unrelated race found during investigation was fixed separately in OPAL-200.

topic: Learning to implement analyses with the framework API
what: Applying a framework's analysis infrastructure to program representations other than the one it is designed for, such as source-level Clang CFGs.
why: PhASAR is designed to analyze compiled LLVM IR and builds its CFGs from it. Converting arbitrary source-level CFGs into IR is outside the framework's scope; it only offers the reverse IR-to-source mapping.
how: No code change. The maintainer suggested compiling to LLVM IR, letting PhASAR build the CFG, and using its IR-to-source mapping to relate results to source-level call sites.

topic: Learning to implement analyses with the framework API
what: Learning how to query data dependencies between program variables using the framework's graph representations.
why: To know how the analysis works
how: No code change. The maintainer pointed to the wiki and to LLVM's def-use chains for scalars. The user's follow-up about taint-style queries was not answered, and the issue remains open.

topic: Learning to implement analyses with the framework API
what: Identifying which framework data structure provides the program information needed by a client analysis, such as the order of calls within a function.
why: PTACallGraph records only caller-callee edges per call site and does not reflect control-flow order, which is captured in the ICFG. Which graph carries which information is not evident from the API.
how: No code change. The maintainer confirmed that the call graph carries no ordering and that the ICFG is the appropriate structure for extracting call order.

topic: Learning to implement analyses with the framework API
what: Using custom LLVM context to query points-to information
why: ContextCond expects a sequence of call-site IDs from the PTACallGraph, but the user pushed PAG node IDs, which do not denote any call site, so no context matched. The expected content of a context is not apparent from the API.
how: No code change. The maintainer showed how to obtain a CallSiteID with PTACallGraph::getCallSiteID() and push it into the ContextCond, which the user confirmed worked.

topic: Learning to implement analyses with the framework API
what: Extending an existing pointer analysis and feeding its newly resolved indirect-call targets back into the framework's call graph.
why: How to extend a pointer analysis and update PTACallGraph with its results is not documented, so the user had to reverse-engineer the extension point from the source.
how: No code change. The maintainer confirmed that addIndirectCallGraphEdge is the right approach and advised verifying the added edges by printing the call graph; the user then got it working.

topic: Learning to implement analyses with the framework API
what: Mapping source-level locations to the framework's internal program representation when combining framework APIs with user-written LLVM code.
why: The user's line-to-value function loaded the bitcode in a separate LLVM context, so the returned llvm::Value was not a key of SVF's LLVMInst2SVFInst map. getSVFValue() implicitly requires values from SVF's own module, and SVF has no API to look up values by file and line.
how: No code change. The maintainer advised building the line-to-value map from the LLVM module built inside SVF, pointed to getLLVMValue() and source-location parsing for the reverse mapping, and confirmed that the SVFG encodes whole-program data dependencies.

topic: Configuring the framework and its options
what: Configuring and running built-in analyses so that they produce visible results.
why: undetermined
how: Unresolved. The maintainer recommended the development branch and reading the code, and the issue was later closed at the reporter's request without a diagnosis or code change.

topic: Configuring the framework and its options
what: Correctly specifying analysis configuration, such as taint sources, sinks and sanitizers, when the configuration format's semantics are not documented.
why: The taint configuration JSON schema listed only field names and types without describing their meaning, e.g., that function names must be the (possibly mangled) LLVM IR names and that parameter indices are zero-based.
how: Added description entries for each field to TaintConfigSchema.json. The maintainer adjusted the wording to keep the build working and merged the change.

topic: Configuring the framework and its options
what: Integrating framework analyses into external tool pipelines that do not provide the configuration the framework implicitly expects.
why: WPAPass only runs the pointer analyses selected by a command-line option such as -ander. When used from another pass manager without that option, no analysis ran, the PAG was never initialized, and alias() dereferenced a null PAG. The framework did not check that an analysis was selected.
how: The maintainer explained that a pointer-analysis option must be specified; the user instead instantiated AndersenWaveDiff directly. In the linked PR SVF-160, an assertion was added to WPAPass::runOnModule that aborts with "No pointer analysis is specified", turning the silent segfault into an explicit error.

topic: Configuring the framework and its options
what: Maintaining a discoverable, consistent and reusable set of configuration options as the framework grows.
why: Command-line options had been added ad hoc as file-local static objects across about 40 source files, without a central registry or naming convention, resulting in scattered and inconsistently named options.
how: Moved all option definitions into static members of the Options class and replaced their uses. Following review, internal names and user-facing option names were made consistent (lowercase hyphenated), with a companion Test-Suite PR updating scripts to the new names.

what: Allowing client analyses to handle calls that the framework cannot resolve, while preserving a clean separation between control-flow and data-flow components.
why: By design, PhASAR separates control-flow information from the data-flow problem; flow functions cannot change control flow, so there is no hook to expose calls the ICFG could not resolve.
how: No code change. The maintainer declined the requested hook and advised implementing a custom ICFG; the reporter worked around the problem with a custom call resolver derived from OTFResolver.

what: Designing framework APIs that hide internal protocols and minimize boilerplate in client analyses and solvers.
why: The sparse-CFG API exposed its internal two-level protocol (per-function, per-fact sparse CFGs with nullable successor queries), so every client and solver had to reimplement the same multi-step boilerplate to advance to the next relevant instruction.
how: Added advanceToNextUser() to the sparse ICFG and its view, backed by a new SparseLLVMControlFlow helper that always returns a non-null instruction, and integrated it into IterativeIDESolver using a C++20 concept to detect supporting ICFGs.

what: Providing APIs to derive and export customized subgraphs of program representations, such as the ICFG nodes reachable from a function.
why: Undetermined. The ICFG class offers no public API for building a new ICFG or editing nodes and edges, and the cause of the user's errors when removing nodes was not diagnosed (likely iterator invalidation while removing edges during iteration).
how: Unresolved. No maintainer response; another user shared a workaround that filters the generated dot file with a Python script.

what: Supporting extensibility of core data structures, such as points-to set representations, without harming readability or runtime performance.
why: PointsTo is a tagged union over a closed set of bit-vector classes with hand-written if/else dispatch in every operation; virtual classes are avoided for backward compatibility and performance, so each new representation must be added at every dispatch site.
how: Not merged. The maintainer rejected the macro-based approach as harming readability and questioned the need for extensibility; SVF still uses the if/else dispatch.

topic: Understanding analysis semantics and framework internals
what: Understanding which analysis techniques a framework supports beyond its core analyses.
why: At the time, PhASAR only used LLVM's flow-insensitive points-to information and supported only data-flow analysis and its required helper analyses; a precise on-demand points-to analysis was still under development, and symbolic execution was out of scope.
how: No code change. The maintainer explained that neither feature was available and pointed to ongoing work on a precise on-demand points-to analysis.

topic: Understanding analysis semantics and framework internals
what: Understanding the precision trade-offs of an analysis to correctly interpret missing or imprecise results.
why: Saber does not perform strong updates, so the first allocation still reaches the later use and the leak is not reported. This is a deliberate precision trade-off of Saber's sparse value-flow analysis, not a defect in memory SSA.
how: No code change. The maintainer explained weak updates, pointed to the SVF paper for definitions of top-level and address-taken variables, and noted that the demand-driven SUPA analysis can handle such strong updates.

topic: Understanding analysis semantics and framework internals
what: Understanding how framework components divide responsibilities, such as which properties are encoded in the graph and which are applied by the solver.
why: This is expected by design: the SVFG does not encode strong updates, so the edge from the first store is always in the graph. The flow-sensitive solver does apply strong updates and does not propagate points-to sets along that edge when the store target is a singleton.
how: No code change. The maintainer explained the division of labor between the SVFG and the flow-sensitive analysis.

topic: Understanding analysis semantics and framework internals
what: Selecting the analysis whose semantics match the program behavior of interest, such as multi-threaded execution.
why: No defect in SVF: Andersen's analysis reports the expected alias, but the flow-sensitive analysis the reporter used is not thread-sensitive, and under thread interleaving the test does not guarantee aliasing.
how: No code change. The maintainer explained the differences between Andersen, the flow-sensitive analysis and the MTA analysis. The question about plans for a thread-sensitive flow-sensitive analysis was not answered.

topic: Understanding analysis semantics and framework internals
what: Correctly traversing the framework's program graph to implement custom client analyses, such as backward taint tracking.
why: To know whether backward analysis breaks SVF PAG
how: No code change. The maintainer walked through the memcpy encoding in the PAG and suggested -model-arrays=true; the user resolved the problem by handling copy and reverse edges in their traversal.

topic: Understanding analysis semantics and framework internals
what: Understanding when and why indirect call sites remain unresolved in the constructed call graph.
why: Indirect call targets are resolved from the points-to set of the function pointer; when the analysis computes an empty points-to set, the call site has no resolved callees. This is the intended semantics of on-the-fly call graph construction.
how: No code change. The maintainer confirmed the user's code was correct, showed how to obtain callers and callees, and explained the empty points-to case.

what: Presenting analysis results in a uniform and user-understandable form, including mapping results back to source code.
why: The framework offered no reporting hook, so result presentation was scattered across the analysis driver and per-analysis print functions, and results were expressed purely in terms of LLVM IR without source-level information.
how: Added a virtual report hook to the IFDS/IDE problem interfaces that the solvers call after solving, and a new LLVMIRToSrc utility that derives source locations from debug metadata. Existing analyses implemented the hook, and hard-coded printing was removed from AnalysisController.

what: Providing consistent, human-readable result reports across all analyses offered by the framework.
why: The project lacked resources to implement proper emitTextReport() methods for all analyses, so some IFDS analyses fell back to the base-class default that prints 'No text report available!'.
how: No code change. The maintainer pointed to the existing --emit-raw-results option and invited contributions; the issue was closed as wontfix.

what: Reporting analysis warnings at an appropriate granularity, avoiding redundant or duplicated reports while retaining the information needed to understand them.
why: undetermined
how: undetermined

what: Making analysis configuration choices observable to support debugging of analysis runs.
why: ContextProviderKey.compute() selected the ContextProvider without reporting it, and ContextProvider and the type iterators lacked informative toString methods, so the chosen configuration was invisible to users.
how: Added a log message naming the selected ContextProvider and toString overrides for ContextProvider, CallStringContextProvider and CFA_k_l_TypeIterator so that the log shows the configuration.

what: Exposing solver internals and performance statistics to support debugging and tuning of data-flow analyses.
why: Edge functions and jump functions were stored in internal solver caches without iteration or summary interfaces, and EdgeFunction lacked hashing and equality support, so neither users nor the AnalysisController could inspect them.
how: Added edge-function hashing and equality, a cache visitor, and a new EdgeFunctionStats class reporting counts, kinds and composition depths of edge and jump functions. AnalysisController prints these statistics and the solver time when requested.

what: Relating internal identifiers in analysis graphs and dumps back to the original program representation to support debugging.
why: SymbolTableInfo kept the value-to-SymID and object-to-SymID maps internally without a way to list them, so users could not determine which LLVM value a SymID represents.
how: This PR was closed and resubmitted; the final version (SVF-393) added SymbolTableInfo::dump(), invoked with a new --print-symbol-table option, which prints each SymID with its symbol type and LLVM value.

what: Providing convenient ways to inspect and visualize analysis graphs while debugging.
why: The constraint-graph display mode was hard-coded, the non-brief labels printed whole functions, and ConstraintGraph and CHGraph offered no interactive view. NormalGepPE was also mislabeled due to a copy-paste error.
how: Added view() methods for ConstraintGraph and CHGraph to display them from a debugger, a -brief-constraint-graph option controlling node labels, concise labels in non-brief mode, and a corrected NormalGepPE label.

what: Enabling and discovering the framework's debug output facilities.
why: SVF does not document how to enable its DBOUT output; DBOUT builds on LLVM's debug macro and is enabled through LLVM's -debug-only mechanism rather than through a debugger.
how: No code change. The maintainer suggested -debug-only with links to external resources, and another user pointed to the LLVM Programmer's Manual.

what: Supporting path- and value-sensitive reasoning, such as call-graph reachability that accounts for argument values and branch conditions.
why: SVF's call-graph reachability is path-insensitive and does not track branch conditions guarding calls. Achieving the required precision would need encoding constraints for an SMT solver, which SVF did not implement.
how: Unresolved. The maintainer acknowledged the limitation, invited a contribution, and suggested encoding conditions on the SVFG using SVF's existing path-condition implementation as a starting point.

what: Supporting implicit-flow taint analysis that combines control dependencies with value flows.
why: SVF does not support implicit taint analysis; its SVFG captures only data dependencies, not control dependencies from branch or loop conditions.
how: Unresolved. The maintainer acknowledged the limitation and suggested reasoning about loop bounds with LLVM's scalar evolution analysis as a possible route for the user's own implementation.

what: Maintaining complete and portable build configurations as third-party dependencies and toolchains evolve.
why: The link commands of the dvf and saber tools omitted the thread library, although the statically linked Z3 library calls pthread_create, so linking failed.
how: The reporter opened PR SVF-737 adding pthread to the link libraries of the affected tools, but closed it unmerged. No other fix was recorded.

what: Ensuring that resource-management features, such as global cache flushing, preserve the identity invariants that other framework components rely on.
why: undetermined
how: undetermined

what: Avoiding conflicts with other libraries when extending standard-library facilities in public framework headers.
why: SVF specialized std::hash for all std::pair types globally in a public header, so any other library defining the same specialization caused a conflicting redefinition in client code using both.
how: Introduced an SVF-scoped SVF::Hash template that keeps the existing pair hashing and falls back to std::hash otherwise, switched SVF's containers and hashers to it, and removed the global std::hash specialization. Performance was shown to be unchanged.

what: Preserving backward compatibility for existing integration paths when refactoring framework abstractions.
why: A refactoring that introduced the SVFModule abstraction removed WPAPass's LLVM module-pass functionality, breaking users that run SVF through LLVM opt. DDAPass also did not correctly convert the LLVM Module into an SVFModule.
how: The reporter contributed two merged PRs: SVF-290 restored WPAPass as a registered LLVM ModulePass that builds an SVFModule from the LLVM Module, and SVF-291 added the same bridge to DDAPass.

what: Providing accurate assertions and informative diagnostics for valid analysis configurations.
why: undetermined
how: undetermined

what: Maintaining integration tests whose expected results must evolve as analysis precision and soundness improve.
why: The integration tests are snapshot tests encoding the exact set of reachable methods. Two call-graph improvements (OPAL-237 and OPAL-229) made more methods reachable, breaking the stored expectations; the varying failure counts reflected which PRs were merged, not nondeterminism.
how: Fix the implementation and integration tests

what: Detecting memory errors and leaks in the framework through continuous integration, within the resource limits of CI platforms.
why: The CI had no sanitizer build, so memory errors stemming from unclear object ownership in manual memory management went unnoticed. The large performance test also exceeded the CI memory limit under the sanitizer.
how: Added a sanitizer build option and an AddressSanitizer CI job, and fixed the reported errors mostly by using stack objects or std::unique_ptr and clarifying ownership. The large performance test was skipped under ASAN in favor of a smaller test; CI failed after merging because the smaller test was not found, with no recorded follow-up.

what: Keeping user-facing documentation up to date with the framework so new users can learn how to run analyses.
why: The phasar.org website and much of the wiki were no longer maintained alongside the code and lacked or contained outdated instructions for running PhASAR.
how: No documentation change. The maintainer redirected the reporter to less outdated wiki pages and closed the issue as a duplicate of existing documentation issues, which remain open.

what: Organizing the codebase so that application-specific components are separated from the reusable library layer.
why: The AnalysisController, used only by the phasar-cli tool, was shipped as a library component, mixing tool code with library code, breaking the project's folder convention, and forcing library users to compile it.
how: Moved the AnalysisController sources into the phasar-cli tool, removed the phasar_controller library target, simplified the controller, and documented the breaking change.

what: Keeping header dependencies minimal and acyclic so that components can be included without pulling in unrelated parts of the framework.
why: Widely used pointer-analysis enums were nested inside heavyweight analysis classes, so Options.h had to include the full pointer-analysis stack, creating long transitive include chains and a circular include once a graph header needed Options.h.
how: Extracted the enums into a standalone PTATY.h header, made Options.h include only lightweight headers, updated all enum uses, and added the explicit includes that files had previously relied on transitively.

what: maintenance, MSli support to the MTA flow-sensitive analysis path
why: undetermined
how: undetermined

what: Releasing research analysis implementations as open source when they are subject to external constraints.
why: The SUPA implementation involved a company's intellectual property, so it could not be merged into the open-source repository.
how: No code change. The maintainer stated that SUPA would not be merged at that stage.

what: Retaining source-level debug information, such as line numbers and local variable names, when loading compiled classes.
why: dbg info not retained by default
how: Unresolved. Nobody answered; a maintainer later closed the issue for inactivity.

what: Preserving accurate source line information when translating bytecode into the framework's IR, including statements created or rewritten by IR transformations.
why: Dexpler's DexReturnInliner replaced a goto-to-return with a cloned return statement without copying the original unit's tags, dropping or misplacing line numbers. In addition, not every DEX instruction has its own debug line entry, so units built from them received no line tag.
how: DexBody.jimplify now assigns the last valid line number to units without one when keep_line_number is on, and DexReturnInliner copies the replaced unit's tags onto the cloned return statement. The PR was closed without discussion, and whether it was merged is not recorded.

what: Preserving source line information for all instruction kinds when translating bytecode into the framework's IR.
why: In the Dexpler frontend, the jimplify code of the goto marker, if-test, if-test-zero and sparse-switch instructions never called addTags(), so the units they produced had no line-number tag and reported -1.
how: Added the missing addTags() calls in the four Dexpler instruction classes so these units carry line numbers from the DEX debug information. The reporter of the linked issue confirmed the fix.

what: Retaining original source variable names in the framework's IR.
why: By default, Soot names locals with its own scheme (r0, $i0, ...) and uses the original names only when an opt-in option is enabled.
how: No code change. A maintainer pointed to an existing option but, when asked about the Java API, named set_keep_line_number(true), which controls line numbers rather than names; the documented option is the jb phase option use-original-names. The issue was closed without correction or confirmation.

what: Recovering distinct source-level variables from bytecode whose local-variable slots are reused and whose debug information may be inconsistent.
why: The ASM frontend caches Jimple locals by bytecode local-variable index. javac reuses an index for variables with disjoint scopes, so both source variables map to one Local and one name. Splitting locals using only the local variable table is unsafe because that table may be inconsistent, e.g., in obfuscated code.
how: Unresolved. A contributor proposed running the LocalSplitter before renaming or attaching temporary name tags to definitions, but nobody chose a design, and the issue remains open.

what: Retaining original source variable names in decompiled output.
why: By default, Soot builds Jimple without original variable names; they are kept only when the jb phase option use-original-names is set before classes are loaded, and later optimizations may still lose them.
how: No code change. A maintainer explained how to set use-original-names on the command line and through the Java API, and warned that Dava is unstable and poorly supported. The issue remains open without confirmation.

what: Robustly handling debug information that does not correspond to the converted instructions when recovering original variable names.
why: tryCorrectingLocalNames assumed every local-variable-table index with several entries also had a Local in the locals map, but that map is filled only for indices referenced by converted instructions. An unused index produced a null value that was dereferenced.
how: Added a guard that skips local-variable indices without an entry in the locals map. The linked issue was closed together with the PR, consistent with a merge.

what: Mapping source-level locations to IR instructions to seed client analyses such as slicing.
why: WALA has no direct lookup from source line to IR instruction index, and the relation between IR indices, bytecode indices and source positions is not obvious from the API. The user passed the SSA instruction index to getSourcePosition(), which expects a bytecode index.
how: No code change. A maintainer explained how to iterate over IR instructions to find the matching line and pointed to the wiki page on mapping IR indices to bytecode indices and source lines; the user then built the seed statement.

what: Correctly mapping IR instructions back to source line numbers.
why: Usage error: the user passed the SSA instruction index to getSourcePosition(), which expects a bytecode index; the two numberings differ.
how: No code change. A maintainer told the user to convert the IR index with getBytecodeIndex() first and linked the wiki page; the user confirmed this fixed the problem.

topic: Handling incomplete code and missing dependencies
what: Analyzing applications whose library dependencies are not available in the analysis scope.
why: The referenced library classes were neither in the APKs nor on the Soot classpath, and Soot by default refuses to continue when it cannot resolve a referenced class.
how: No code change. A maintainer pointed to the existing -allow-phantom-refs option, which creates phantom classes for missing references at the cost of an incomplete program; the reporter confirmed it worked.

topic: Handling incomplete code and missing dependencies
what: Controlling which classes are loaded and with what level of detail when configuring the analysis scope.
why: Exclusions only mark classes as library classes and do not prevent body loading unless -no-bodies-for-excluded is set, inclusions take precedence over exclusions, and Soot resolves unreferenced classes lazily only to the HIERARCHY level. The later DANGLING exception was a separate regression introduced by a recent merge.
how: Only the regression was fixed (commit 92a0d48). For the original request, a maintainer suggested Scene.forceResolve with the SIGNATURES level, and maintainers agreed phantom members should be created with --allow-phantom-refs, but no change is recorded and the issue remains open.

topic: Handling incomplete code and missing dependencies
what: Configuring a complete classpath so that all classes referenced by the analyzed application can be resolved.
why: The library providing the missing class (AXmlPrinter2.jar) was not on the classpath. The cause of the later DANGLING errors was not identified because the maintainer could not reproduce them.
how: No code change. A maintainer advised adding the missing jar to the classpath, using -pp (unsound for Android), or using -allow-phantom-refs. The follow-up errors were closed as not reproducible.

topic: Handling incomplete code and missing dependencies
what: Ensuring that library classes on the classpath are fully loaded so that implicit calls, such as static initializers, appear in the call graph.
why: In the simplified example the behavior was correct, since the call chain goes through <clinit>. In the real case, the surrounding test framework excluded the classes from the Soot scene, so the class was marked phantom and its <clinit> had no body or edges.
how: No code change. Maintainers explained the expected call chain and guided the reporter through debugging the resolver; the reporter found the exclusion in their test framework and then saw the expected edge.

topic: Handling incomplete code and missing dependencies
what: Tolerating incomplete class hierarchies, such as generated classes whose superclasses are missing from the classpath, instead of crashing.
why: SootClass.getSuperclass() assumed every non-phantom class has a superclass and threw otherwise, and BytecodeHierarchy.buildAncestryTree called it without checking. Generated non-phantom classes with unavailable superclasses violated this assumption, and -ignore-resolution-errors was not consulted.
how: Guarded the exception in getSuperclass() with the ignore_resolution_errors option so null is returned when it is enabled, and added a superclass check in buildAncestryTree. A maintainer noted that generating phantom superclasses would be the long-term solution.

topic: Handling incomplete code and missing dependencies
what: Representing calls to code outside the analysis scope in the call graph.
why: Only one JAR was given to Soot, so the callee classes of some call sites had no definition and the call graph builder could not create edges to them.
how: No code change. A maintainer pointed to the existing -allow-phantom-refs option; the reporter did not confirm, and the issue remains open.

topic: Handling incomplete code and missing dependencies
what: Preserving the original program's runtime semantics when generating code for unresolved method references.
why: For unresolvable methods, Soot synthesized a stub that throws a plain java.lang.Error, whereas the JVM raises NoSuchMethodError at link time. The original program relied on catching NoSuchMethodError, so the stub changed its behavior.
how: set -allow-phantom-refs option or update soot version

topic: Handling incomplete code and missing dependencies
what: Robustly constructing call graphs when allocated types cannot be resolved in the class hierarchy.
why: ClassHierarchy.lookupClass returns null for types missing from the scope, but AbstractRootMethod.addAllocation used the result for array types before its null check, assuming every allocated type resolves.
how: Local code fix

topic: Handling incomplete code and missing dependencies
what: Generating control-flow graphs from source code whose dependencies are not available.
why: Undetermined. Another user reported that missing dependencies make the polyglot source front end produce incorrect CFGs for some methods, but no cause was identified.
how: use polyglot

topic: Handling incomplete code and missing dependencies
what: Analyzing source code whose dependencies are missing from the analysis scope.
why: The JDT-based source front end is not robust to missing classes: JDT returns null bindings for unresolvable types, which the translator dereferences, although WALA's class hierarchy itself tolerates missing classes.
how: Unresolved. The maintainer knew no workaround and suggested analyzing bytecode instead. Null checks proposed in the related issue WALA-99 only moved the NPE elsewhere, and the issue remains open.

what: edges missing for async callbacks
why: All AsyncTask callbacks shared the ASYNCTASK edge kind, which links arguments and return values to every callee, failing for void callbacks. The XML summary format cannot express parameter or return-value mappings, and edges with the same source signature overwrite each other.
how: A maintainer committed a quick fix (288a07b) that keeps the ASYNCTASK edge kind only for parameter-passing callbacks and uses GENERIC_FAKE for the others; the reporter's PR SOOT-1702 added a test. Extending the XML format with parameter and return mappings remains open.

what: Keeping library models up to date with evolving language built-ins and platform APIs.
why: Undetermined. The PR does not state a cause; the patch suggests the hand-written JavaScript models covered only older ECMAScript and DOM APIs, so calls to newer built-ins had no target.
how: Extended prologue.js and preamble.js with stubs for newer built-ins and DOM methods (e.g., Map, Set, Proxy, Promise, Object.defineProperty), many with placeholder bodies, and made Array sort call its comparator.

topic: Modeling entry points and program initialization
what: Modeling framework-invoked callbacks, such as Android listener methods, as entry points in call graph construction.
why: onClick() is a framework callback with no caller in the app code, so it requires FlowDroid's dummy main, which identifies callbacks from AndroidCallbacks.txt. The reporter had not copied this file into their project, so no callbacks were included.
how: No code change. Maintainers advised using FlowDroid's dummy main construction; the reporter fixed their setup by copying AndroidCallbacks.txt into the project.

topic: Modeling entry points and program initialization
what: Correctly modeling implicit static initialization, including superclass static initializers, in call graph construction.
why: EntryPoints.clinitsOf() looked up <clinit> only on the class itself instead of walking up the superclass chain as documented, so edges to superclass static initializers were missing. The interface case was not a bug, since constant fields need no static initializer.
how: PR SOOT-1610 changed clinitsOf() to walk up the superclass chain to the first <clinit>, made the call graph builder skip self-edges from static initializers, and added tests.

topic: Modeling entry points and program initialization
what: Configuring entry points to include methods that are not reachable from the program's main method.
why: Soot builds the call graph only from the configured entry points (by default main), and the user was unaware that entry points can be configured. Why some methods were still not entry points was not determined.
how: No code change. The maintainer pointed to the wiki on custom entry points and advised setting all methods as entry points via Scene.setEntryPoints. The follow-up problem remained unresolved.

topic: Modeling entry points and program initialization
what: Ensuring deterministic entry-point discovery and call graph construction across repeated runs.
why: Class loaders stored module entries in a TreeSet ordered by hash codes, and DexModuleEntry did not implement hashCode()/equals(). Identity hash codes changing between runs altered the set of loaded classes and hence the discovered entry points.
how: PR WALA-134 removed HashCodeComparator and iterated directly over module entries, and added hashCode() and equals() to DexModuleEntry.

topic: Modeling entry points and program initialization
what: Modeling test-framework entry points across evolving framework conventions.
why: Test methods are invoked reflectively by the JUnit runner, and JUnitEntryPoints only recognized the JUnit 3 convention, not the annotations used by JUnit 4 and 5.
how: Added recognition of JUnit 4 and JUnit 5 annotations so annotated test, setup and teardown methods are added as entry points. Whether the PR was merged is not recorded.

topic: Modeling entry points and program initialization
what: Including entry-point methods in the call graph when their parameter types are outside the analysis scope.
why: For dataflow-based call graph builders, an entry point is called from the fake root method only if a concrete type can be allocated for every parameter; when a parameter type is missing, the call is silently omitted.
how: No code change. The maintainer explained the behavior and suggested a custom Entrypoint subclass passing null for unresolvable parameters, or the less precise CHACallGraph.

what: Keeping IR construction passes consistent in their assumptions so that the resulting IR is well-typed.
why: The LocalSplitter and UnreachableCodeEliminator built their control-flow graphs with different exception settings, so they disagreed on whether an exception handler was reachable. The resulting local split mixed types, and the type assigner produced an ill-typed cast that SPARK rejected.
how: fixes in unreachable code detection

what: Supporting optimized or protected bytecode formats in the frontend.
why: Dexpler does not support optimized (odex) opcodes, which call methods through vtable indices and require register type information that is unavailable until much later in body construction. APK protectors may introduce further unsupported constructs.
how: Unresolved. The maintainer acknowledged that odex opcode support should be implemented, but no code change followed and the issue remains open.

what: Keeping input parsers compatible with evolving platform toolchains and file formats.
why: The bundled axmlprinter binary-XML parser, derived from an old unmaintained project, has a long-known defect triggered by manifests produced by Android Studio 3.0 and later.
how: Replaced the axmlprinter-based manifest parsing with the pxb AxmlReader (commit 3e8dced). A contributor's equivalent PR SOOT-819 was closed unmerged in favor of the maintainers' patch.

what: Printing IR statements robustly when control-flow targets form cycles between statements.
why: JLookupSwitchStmt.toString and JTableSwitchStmt.toString printed each case target by calling the target unit's own toString, special-casing only self-targets. When a case jumped to another switch statement whose targets led back, printing recursed endlessly and caused a StackOverflowError.
how: PR soot-2234 added an AbstractSwitchStmt.appendTarget helper that prints 'self' for self-targets and a placeholder for targets that are switch statements instead of recursing; both switch statement classes use it.

what: Building IR from source code robustly when the underlying front end cannot resolve all bindings.
why: The JDT translator assumed every AST binding resolves, but JDT returns null bindings when referenced libraries are missing from the analysis scope and, even with all jars present, for some constructs (possibly a JDT bug). Unlike the rest of WALA, the source front end does not degrade gracefully.
how: Unresolved. The maintainer suggested null checks and invited a PR, but bailing out only moved the NPE elsewhere. As workarounds, the maintainer proposed catching the NPE or using the more robust bytecode front end; the reporter switched to a different approach.

what: Exposing bytecode-level metadata, such as constant field initializers, through the framework's IR and APIs.
why: Compile-time constant fields are initialized through the class file's ConstantValue attribute rather than code in <clinit>, and WALA neither translates that attribute into IR nor exposes it through the IField interface.
