how: No code change. The maintainer explained a workaround: cast the IClass to ShrikeClass and read the field's ConstantValue attribute through the Shrike ClassReader, which the user confirmed works.

what: Supporting new language versions and constructs, such as ES6, in the framework's language front ends.
why: WALA's JavaScript front end does not support ES6: although Rhino can parse it, each ES6 construct must also be translated from the Rhino AST into WALA IR, which had not been implemented.
how: No code change in WALA. The reporter changed the Rhino language setting in their local copy to handle 'let'; full ES6 support was acknowledged as a major effort.

what: Constructing pointer assignment graphs robustly from IR produced by bytecode-to-IR conversion of real-world apps.
why: Undetermined. The maintainer could not obtain the APK; the crash suggests a cast operand typed as a primitive long reached the PAG builder, possibly due to a typing problem in Dalvik-to-Jimple conversion, but this was not confirmed.
how: Unresolved. The maintainer asked for the APK and whether the problem persisted; the reporter did not respond, and the issue remains open.

what: Constructing SSA form and dominator information for unusual control-flow graphs, such as those produced by obfuscated code.
why: missing first element in ArrayPackedset.toList
how: Fixed tolist

what: Generating verifiable bytecode after SSA-based transformations in the presence of exception handlers.
why: Shimple's phi elimination inserted copies at the end of predecessor blocks, but ExceptionalUnitGraph did not add an exceptional edge from the first trapped unit to the handler when that unit could not throw. The copy therefore landed inside the trap, while the JVM verifier assumes the handler may be reached before any trapped statement executes.
how: PR soot-681 changed ExceptionalUnitGraph so that the first unit of every trap always gets an exceptional edge to its handler, placing phi-elimination copies before the trap. It was merged about 3.5 years after the report.

what: Preserving program metadata, such as declared exceptions, when writing transformed programs back to an executable format.
why: The DEX reader converted the dalvik.annotation.Throws annotation into the method's exception list rather than an annotation tag, while DexPrinter only serialized annotation tags. The asymmetric handling meant the writer never turned the exception list back into the annotation.
how: Extended DexPrinter to emit a Throws annotation listing the method's declared exceptions. The author explained that the reader never keeps Throws as a generic annotation, so round trips cannot duplicate it. The PR was merged.

what: Ensuring that output-generation algorithms, such as long-jump splitting in DEX output, terminate on large real-world code.
why: A regression in the long-jump splitter: when a jump exceeded the maximum DEX offset, insertIntermediateJump placed the intermediate jump next to the original one and, when that position was unusable, moved it away from the target, so splitting never converged.
how: A maintainer fixed insertIntermediateJump in commit cc7306dc to search for a free position towards the target instead of away from it. The reporter confirmed the fix.

what: Supporting multi-file program formats, such as multi-dex APKs, both when loading programs and when writing transformed output.
why: Soot lacked both features: it loaded classes from only one dex file, and it had no dex splitter, so the instrumented program written into a single dex file exceeded the format's limits.
how: Only loading was addressed: PR soot-580 added an opt-in process-multiple-dex option to read all dex files of an APK. Dex splitting for output remained unsupported; maintainers acknowledged it and invited contributions.

what: Keeping analysis-oriented configuration from silently affecting the completeness of generated output programs.
why: FlowDroid overwrote Soot's options for call-graph construction, excluding packages such as android.* and java.*. Soot did not load the excluded classes, so they were missing from the written APK, causing it to crash at run time. A second user's corrupted output was caused by the Android API level setting.
how: No code change. The maintainer suggested a custom configuration that includes all classes and multiple dex files; the reporter instead re-initialized the Soot configuration after call-graph construction. The second user fixed their output by setting the Android API version.

what: Ensuring that randomized program transformations, such as obfuscation, always produce valid code.
why: When the GotoInstrumenter's randomly chosen chunk contained only one statement, the code building the new try-catch could not find an end statement and created a trap with a null end unit, which failed body validation.
how: Rewrote GotoInstrumenter to skip small and special methods, retry choosing a chunk boundary outside existing traps, compute the trap's end unit explicitly, and skip the try-catch when no valid range exists. The PR was merged.

what: Preserving source-language semantics when simplifying decompiled code.
why: The Dava transformation removing empty default constructors treated any empty no-argument constructor as compiler-generated, also removing explicitly declared non-public constructors that restrict instantiation.
how: Added a visibility check so that non-public empty constructors are kept, and moved the Dava output call into PackManager.writeOutput() for easier debugging. The PR was merged.

what: Generating output files that respect platform constraints, such as filesystem filename length limits.
why: SourceLocator named Jimple/Shimple output files after the fully qualified class name in a single path component, so deeply nested inner classes exceeded the 255-character filename limit.
how: Added an opt-in -hierarchy-dirs option that writes Jimple/Shimple output into package directories instead of flat files.

what: Handling output-size limits of target platforms when generating programs for legacy runtimes.
why: MultiDexBuilder splits output into multiple dex files only for API level 22 and above; for older targets, splitting would require computing the main-dex classes, which Soot does not implement, so it threw an exception on overflow.
how: Not merged. The maintainers decided no new option was needed and instead replaced the exception with a warning that the app will not run on older devices (PR soot-2249).

topic: Modeling reflection and dynamic language features
what: Modeling the full range of reflective calls recorded in dynamic reflection logs.
why: The exception for unknown reflection-log entries is deliberate: Soot's ReflectiveCallsInliner does not model these kinds of reflective calls, so merely loading the named classes would mask the missing modeling.
how: Not merged. The maintainer argued the patch masks the problem; the contributor withdrew the PR and kept using the TamiFlex configuration recommended for Soot.

topic: Modeling reflection and dynamic language features
what: Analyzing dynamically loaded code, such as secondary dex files loaded at run time, to achieve complete code coverage.
why: Secondary dex files are loaded at run time through DexClassLoader and accessed via reflection. Soot neither determines which file is loaded nor merges its classes into the Scene, and its reflection support only partly covers this interaction.
how: Unresolved. Maintainers suggested extracting secondary dex files and analyzing them as well, and proposed an option to merge all dex files of an APK into the Scene, but no implementation is recorded.

topic: Modeling reflection and dynamic language features
what: Correctly checking type compatibility when resolving reflective call targets.
why: OnFlyCallGraphBuilder.isReflectionCompatible passed the arguments of FastHierarchy.canStoreType in reversed order, so reflective calls passing a subtype of the declared parameter type were judged incompatible.
how: still open

topic: Modeling reflection and dynamic language features
what: Keeping up with bytecode features introduced by new Java versions, such as invokedynamic-based string concatenation.
why: Since Java 9, javac compiles string concatenation into invokedynamic calls bootstrapped by StringConcatFactory, but this class was not among Soot's basic classes and was not loaded. The cause of a subsequent Grimp NullPointerException was not identified.
how: PR soot-1315 registered StringConcatFactory as a basic class when running on Java 9 or later. The later Grimp NullPointerException was not addressed by the fix.

topic: Modeling reflection and dynamic language features
what: Preserving program behavior when analysis-oriented models of dynamic features are written back to executable code.
why: Undetermined. The jb.model-lambdametafactory option, enabled by default, replaces lambda invokedynamic calls with a synthetic class modeling LambdaMetafactory for analysis purposes; the written output lacked the lambda body and the synthetic class, but the thread does not explain why.
how: No code change. Another user suggested disabling jb.model-lambdametafactory so that lambdas remain invokedynamic calls.

topic: Modeling reflection and dynamic language features
what: Modeling native and reflective library methods so that pointer analysis and call graphs cover reflective field accesses.
why: According to the reporter, Class.getDeclaredFields() delegates to a native method that Soot's native-method simulation does not model, so no allocation sites are created for the returned fields and Field.get() calls have empty points-to sets.
how: model Class.getDeclaredFields() in spark

topic: Modeling reflection and dynamic language features
what: Exploiting constant arguments of reflective calls to improve call-graph precision.
why: The context for java.lang.Class methods recorded only the receiver type, so the model of getMethod/getDeclaredMethod returned all methods of that type regardless of a constant method-name argument. Constant-string tracking existed only for Class.forName.
how: PR wala-51 added a context, context selector and context interpreter that track the constant method name for getMethod/getDeclaredMethod, registered them in the reflection handling, and added a test.

topic: Modeling reflection and dynamic language features
what: Correctly modeling lambdas and method references, including constructor references and captured values, in call-graph construction.
why: LambdaSummaryClass.makeTrampoline, which synthesizes the method forwarding interface calls to the lambda body, used overlapping value-number counters for captured values and arguments and skipped a slot for constructor references, so arguments were passed to the wrong parameters.
how: A maintainer rewrote the trampoline's parameter wiring, passing the allocated object for constructor references, then captured values, then interface arguments, with an explicit parameter-count check. Method-handle kinds became named constants.

topic: Modeling reflection and dynamic language features
what: Resolving calls to signature-polymorphic methods, such as VarHandle access methods.
why: VarHandle methods are signature-polymorphic, so the call-site selector never matches the declared descriptor. WALA has no handling for signature-polymorphic call sites, so resolution by exact selector fails.
how: Unresolved. A maintainer acknowledged the missing support and invited suggestions or a pull request.

what: Building a complete class hierarchy that includes all loaded classes and interfaces.
why: Undetermined in the issue thread. The reporter's unmerged PR suggests interfaces were never recorded as descendants of java.lang.Object in the Hierarchy constructor; the missing IOException subclasses are not explained.
how: Not merged. The reporter's PR soot-164 included a fix, but its API changes triggered a long compatibility discussion and it was closed as too old. The issue remains open.

what: Querying class hierarchies for library types that are not directly referenced by the analyzed application.
why: Undetermined. The maintainer suggested a possible mistake in how Soot was started; the hierarchy may only include classes loaded into the Scene, but this was not confirmed.
how: Unresolved. The reporter provided a minimal program and setup, but received no further reply, and the issue was closed.

what: Correctly implementing class hierarchy and type lattice operations, such as least common superclass and type meet.
why: getLeastCommonSuperclass compared ancestors against b's superclasses without including b itself, so it skipped b when b was an ancestor of a. PointType.meet also fell back to Object for arrays without checking whether both types were equal.
how: Added an equality check for b in getLeastCommonSuperclass and made PointType.meet return the cone type when both have the same underlying type. The PR was merged.

what: Building class hierarchies consistently across different runtime environments, such as Eclipse plug-in tests.
why: unknown
how: Unresolved. No answer or fix followed, and the issue remains open.

what: Correctly computing inherited methods for interface types.
why: transitive reachability missing
how: Unresolved. No maintainer answered the question, and the issue remains open.

what: Preserving inheritance relationships to library types modeled by summaries during class hierarchy construction.
why: Summary-modeled classes were materialized only when bypass logic was added during call-graph-builder setup, which runs after class hierarchy construction. At that time the supertype did not exist, so subclasses fell back to the root class.
how: Added an extension point to register summary class shells before the class hierarchy is built, using an opt-in superclass attribute in XML summaries and a new class-shell loader interface. Making inherited method bodies execute was left to a follow-up.

what: Producing sound points-to information and call graphs when analyzing libraries whose accessible methods are invoked by unknown clients.
why: Spark assumes a closed world in which every entry into a method is visible. In a library, parameters of public/protected methods that are never called inside the analyzed code receive no allocation nodes, so their points-to sets stay empty and virtual calls on them resolve to no target.
how: Added an opt-in Spark option allocate-params that creates an AnySubType allocation node for every reference-typed parameter of public and protected methods. Similar treatment for this and configurable accessibility arrived later in the library call graph PR Soot-488.

what: Distinguishing identically named program entities defined in different files to keep pointer-analysis results precise.
why: Undetermined. The reporter only speculated that the call-string context was too short; no diagnosis was made.
how: unresolved

what: Correctly applying language dispatch and visibility rules when resolving virtual call targets.
why: Contested. The PR author argued that resolveConcreteDispatch() applies a visibility check that fails for methods declared in package-private interfaces, mixing Java's inheritance rules with dispatch rules. The maintainer disputed that this can occur in valid, compilable Java code and could not reproduce a wrong result.
how: Not merged. The proposed patch skipped the visibility check for interface-declared methods, but the maintainer asked for compilable test code and was not convinced; the PR was closed years later as too old.

what: Producing consistent call graphs for the same program across different input formats, such as class files and APKs.
why: Undetermined. No maintainer analyzed the report.
how: Unresolved. The issue was closed years later as stale without a diagnosis or fix.

what: Modeling implicit runtime behavior, such as JVM-created exceptions, in the call graph without cluttering it with rarely relevant edges.
why: The call graph builder only creates edges for explicit invoke expressions and a few implicit targets. The JVM's implicit allocation and constructor call for exceptions such as ClassCastException has no invoke instruction, and omitting these edges is also deliberate by default to avoid cluttering the call graph.
how: PR Soot-2286 added an opt-in cg option add-exception-edges that adds edges of a new EXCEPTION kind to the constructors of exceptions each unit might throw, together with a more precise throw analysis that drops exceptions that cannot be thrown. The default behavior was left unchanged.

what: Ensuring that customized call-target resolution in subclassed components is honored by the components that delegate to them.
why: BypassMethodTargetSelector used an instanceof check that assumed any ClassHierarchyMethodTargetSelector parent behaves exactly like the CHA lookup already performed. Subclasses overriding getCalleeTarget also matched the check, so their custom resolution was silently ignored.
how: PR WALA-52 replaced the instanceof test with an exact class check and added a comment explaining why.

what: Producing consistent call graphs across different construction algorithms given the same entry points.
why: Undetermined. The maintainer suspected, without investigating, that the synthetic fake root method allocates a receiver object for the entrypoint, making the constructor reachable in RTA and 0-CFA but not in the CHA call graph.
how: Unresolved. The maintainer asked the reporter to print the fake root method's IR to confirm the hypothesis; there was no reply, and the issue remains open.

topic: Correctness and precision of client analyses
what: Ensuring client analyses built on the framework handle all type shapes encountered during data-flow propagation without crashing.
why: Undetermined. The failing cast was located in FlowDroid's taint flow function rather than in Soot, and it was not analyzed further.
how: No code change in Soot. The maintainer redirected the report to FlowDroid's issue tracker and asked the reporter to retry with a newly pushed FlowDroid version; whether this fixed the crash was not reported.

what: Scaling call graph construction to large programs by computing only the parts of the call graph that clients actually need.
why: Spark is a whole-program analysis that eagerly computes the complete call graph, requiring the entire program to be loaded and converted to Jimple. Making it on-demand is algorithmically hard, since interface invokes cannot be resolved precisely without global knowledge and Spark also models implicit calls.
how: Unresolved. A maintainer started an on-demand ICFG, but it remained unsound and was not adopted; the work was later put on hold, and the issue remains open.

what: Running data-flow analyses on very large real-world applications within available memory.
why: Undetermined. Neither the memory consumer nor any configuration problem was diagnosed.
how: Unresolved. After the reporter confirmed the heap size, there was no further response, and the issue was later closed for inactivity.

what: Scaling program slicing over system dependence graphs that include full heap data and control dependencies.
why: The maintainer suspected a fundamental scalability limit rather than a bug: SDG-based slicing with full data and control dependencies is very hard to scale. The specific trigger for this parameter was not investigated.
how: No code change. The maintainer suggested reducing the kinds of dependencies considered and pointed to the documentation on improving pointer-analysis scalability.

what: Balancing completeness of dependence information and scalability in program slicing.
why: Under the default NO_HEAP option, dependencies flowing through heap fields are ignored by design. With heap-aware options, the println seed pulls in much of the standard library, and building PDGs with heap parameter-passing statements exhausts memory, a known scalability limitation of the slicer.
how: No code change. The maintainer suggested more aggressive exclusions, an older standard library, or a custom seed method, which fixed the example but did not scale to more complex programs. The issue was closed as a known limitation.

what: Producing stable, reproducible IR output across separate runs on the same code.
why: Undetermined. The thread does not explain why the local order differs between runs; it only notes that locals are not kept in a stable order and that later jb phases may remove locals after names are assigned.
how: Sorted locals by type and first definition position and re-ran the local name standardizer after all other jb phases. Following maintainer feedback, the behavior was made opt-in through new phase options, and the bundled Jimple path lookup was also made optional.

what: Ensuring thread safety of shared framework data structures when analysis phases run in parallel.
why: Method bodies were converted in parallel, but the Scene's shared class table and class chains were accessed without synchronization, so LambdaMetaFactory could observe classes in an inconsistent state, causing intermittent test failures.
how: PR Soot-1191 made the class table a ConcurrentHashMap, routed class registration and RefType creation through synchronized paths, and synchronized HashChain's methods.

what: Achieving deterministic analysis output without unacceptable memory overhead.
why: The PR assumed that iteration over unordered hash-based collections causes processing order and output to vary between runs. The contributor's experiment later showed that switching collections did not effectively remove the non-determinism, so this is at most part of the cause.
how: unresolved

what: Producing deterministic and reproducible analysis results across repeated runs on the same program and configuration.
why: Undetermined. Another user guessed the non-determinism might be timeout-related.
how: Unresolved. No maintainer responded, and the issue remains open.

what: Generating stable identifiers for synthetic program entities so that results are comparable across runs.
why: Undetermined in the thread. Analyst inference: Soot's LambdaMetaFactory names generated lambda classes with a single global counter while bodies are converted in parallel, so the assigned number depends on thread scheduling.
how: No code change. The maintainer answered that identifiers only need to be consistent within one run, as long as call-graph edges and points-to sets are identical. The follow-up question on where identifiers are generated was not answered, and the issue remains open.

what: Maintaining reliable CI test results in the presence of possible non-determinism.
why: Undetermined. The maintainer attributed the failure to known CI flakiness, possibly non-determinism, without investigation.
how: Unresolved. The flaky test failure was not investigated; the PR's other changes were accepted.

what: Loading all program classes deterministically and completely regardless of object identity and hash codes.
why: Class loaders stored module entries in a TreeSet ordered by a hash-code comparator, which is inconsistent with equals, so distinct entries with colliding hash codes were merged. DexModuleEntry also lacked hashCode()/equals(), so identity hash codes varied the kept entries and their order between runs.
how: PR WALA-134 removed the hash-code comparator, collected module entries into a hash set, and implemented hashCode()/equals() for DexModuleEntry based on its class name, making the related Android call graphs stable.

what: Loading all program classes deterministically and completely regardless of object identity and hash codes.
why: A hash-code comparator in a TreeSet is inconsistent with equals and can merge distinct module entries. DexModuleEntry lacked hashCode()/equals(), so identity hash codes made the kept entries and their order vary between runs.
how: Removed the hash-code comparator, collected module entries into a hash set, and implemented hashCode()/equals() for DexModuleEntry based on its class name. The equality fix was needed in addition to removing the comparator to make Android call graphs stable.

topic: Learning to implement analyses with the framework API
what: Understanding the lifecycle of method bodies across analysis phases and using the corresponding framework APIs correctly.
why: The reporter called getActiveBody(), which only returns already loaded bodies, in a whole-program SceneTransformer that runs before the body packs, where bodies were not yet loaded. The difference between getActiveBody() and retrieveActiveBody() is not stated in the API documentation or the exception message.
how: No code change. The maintainer explained that a SceneTransformer should check isConcrete() and use retrieveActiveBody() when no body is loaded, which solved the problem. The request to improve the Javadoc and exception message was not acted on.

topic: Learning to implement analyses with the framework API

topic: Learning to implement analyses with the framework API
what: Deriving execution-path information from program slices for client analyses.
why: WALA's slicer returns an unordered set of statements and provides no functionality to split a slice into execution paths; this requires combining CFGs with the SDG.
how: No code change. The maintainer explained that the feature does not exist and would have to be built from CFGs and the SDG; another user described their own intra-procedural executable slicer as a possible starting point.

topic: Learning to implement analyses with the framework API
what: Discovering and using framework support for analyzing multi-file programs, such as Node.js modules.
why: Multi-file Node.js analysis is supported only in a separate project that is not published as a Maven artifact and not documented; its usage is shown only in tests.
how: No code change. The maintainer pointed to the com.ibm.wala.cast.js.nodejs project, advised building WALA from source, and referred to an existing test as a usage example.

topic: Configuring the framework and its options
what: Understanding the side effects of configuration options on the framework's internal state.
why: When output options are set, Soot releases method bodies after writing out Jimple files to free memory, so bodies are no longer available afterwards. This default side effect is not apparent from the output options.
how: No code change. The maintainer suggested running without the output options or using the existing -no-writeout-body-releasing option, which solved the problem.

topic: Configuring the framework and its options
what: Correctly configuring the analysis scope so that the framework can locate the classes to analyze.
why: The command line set neither a classpath nor a process directory, so the target bytecode was outside Soot's analysis scope and the class could not be resolved.
how: No code change. The maintainer explained that the bytecode must be passed via the classpath or process-dir options.

topic: Configuring the framework and its options
what: Correctly configuring platform-specific inputs, such as Android platform libraries, for the analysis.
why: The Android jar was passed through the generic -cp option, whereas Soot expects Android platform classes via its dedicated options (-android-jars or -force-android-jar).
how: No code change. The maintainer pointed to the existing -android-jars and -force-android-jar options.

topic: Configuring the framework and its options
what: Correctly configuring the framework to load Android applications and their platform classes.
why: Undetermined. Analyst inference: the APK was not passed through -process-dir and its path contained an unquoted space, so Soot found no APK; this was not confirmed.
how: Unresolved. Only another user replied with a suggestion that changed the error; no maintainer responded, and the issue remains open.

topic: Configuring the framework and its options
what: Correctly configuring the framework so that the class hierarchy of Android applications, including platform classes, is complete.
why: The command line omitted the APK source precedence (-src-prec apk) and the Android platform jars (--android-jars), so framework classes such as the superclass of HttpEntityWrapper were unavailable to the type hierarchy.
how: No code change. The maintainer showed a working command line with these options added and closed the issue.

what: Allowing applications that embed the framework as a library to control its diagnostic output.
why: Soot's output was hard-wired to a global PrintStream (G.v().out) and direct System.out calls guarded by static DEBUG flags, providing no log levels, per-class filtering or pluggable destinations.
how: Not merged. The PR was superseded by SOOT-910, which migrated Soot's output to SLF4J loggers and deprecated G.v().out; the follow-up SOOT-916 restored console output for soot.Main.

what: Designing API signatures that accept the natural types used by client analyses without forcing unsafe casts or copies.
why: Java generics are invariant, and the ReachableMethods and TransitiveTargets signatures used the exact type argument MethodOrMethodContext instead of a bounded wildcard, so an Iterator<SootMethod> was rejected.
how: Widened the parameter types to bounded wildcards (e.g., Iterator<? extends MethodOrMethodContext>) and added missing type arguments. The change is source-compatible for existing callers.

what: Supporting framework extensions, such as plugins, in execution environments with restricted class loading, such as OSGi.
why: PluginLoader hard-wired plugin instantiation to Class.forName(className).newInstance() using Soot's own class loader, with no way for the embedding environment to supply its own loading mechanism.
how: Introduced a ClassLoadingStrategy interface with a default reflection-based implementation and made PluginLoader instantiate plugins through a replaceable strategy set via PluginLoader.setClassLoadingStrategy.

what: Constructing analysis scopes for application types, such as web applications, whose packaging conventions differ from standalone Java applications.
why: Manifest Class-Path handling was hard-wired into AnalysisScopeReader, although it applies only to applications launched with java -jar. For web applications, these entries did not resolve and caused FileNotFoundException.
how: Not merged. The PR added overloads with a readManifest flag, but maintainers asked for a regression test and questioned the usage scenario since J2EE support had been removed. The PR went stale and was closed; WALA still reads manifests unconditionally.

what: Keeping APIs free of redundant overloads and unused parameters as they evolve.
why: An earlier migration toward the nullary getStatements() was left incomplete: subclasses still overrode the deprecated overload taking SSAOptions, and the unused options parameter propagated into constructors of many root and synthetic method classes.
how: Removed getStatements(SSAOptions), moved all overrides to the nullary overload, added options-free constructors, and deprecated the old constructors for removal.

what: Propagating client configuration consistently through all framework layers, including source-code front ends.
why: SSAOptions was not threaded through the chain of components that build IR from source (analysis engines, loader factories, source loaders, translators), so these front ends could not receive a client's pi-node policy.
how: Added an SSAOptions parameter to the source analysis engines, loader factories, source loaders, module translators and AstTranslator, added a CAst instanceof operator, and opened InstanceOfPiPolicy for subclassing. This PR continued the stalled WALA-1798 and was merged.

topic: Understanding analysis semantics and framework internals
what: Understanding how the call graph construction algorithm resolves virtual calls in order to interpret missing edges.
why: SPARK resolves virtual call targets from the allocation sites in the receiver's points-to set. The receiver of getDescription can only be null, so no allocation site exists and no edge is created; this is expected by construction.
how: No code change. The maintainer explained that the missing edge is the expected result of points-to-based call resolution.

topic: Understanding analysis semantics and framework internals
what: Understanding how front-end translation of different input formats, such as Dalvik bytecode, shapes the generated IR.
why: Undetermined. The maintainer stated that the shared local is expected behavior and not a bug, but the thread does not explain why; it likely reflects Dalvik register reuse carried over by Dexpler.
how: No code change. The maintainer redirected the reporter to a FlowDroid discussion; no option to split the local was offered, and the issue remains open.

topic: Understanding analysis semantics and framework internals
what: Understanding how the framework models exceptional control flow generated by the compiler.
why: The unbalanced monitorenter/monitorexit paths are exceptional control flow that javac generates for synchronized blocks and that WALA faithfully models. The reporter's reading of the JVM specification did not account for these exceptional edges.
how: No code change. The maintainer explained both exceptional paths with links to the generated bytecode.

topic: Understanding analysis semantics and framework internals
what: Understanding how language constructs are modeled in the IR in order to interpret call graph results.
why: For uniformity, WALA's JavaScript IR models array and object literals as calls to the Array and Object constructors, so each literal appears as a call site in the call graph.
how: No code change. The maintainer explained the IR modeling and suggested filtering constructor targets by source location on the client side. The issue remains open.

what: Helping analysis developers inspect intermediate solver results to debug their data-flow analyses.
why: The facts computed by the Heros solver are internal state with no view relating them to the analyzed program's code, so analysis designers could not easily see where wrong facts are computed.
how: No code change in Soot. The issue was closed by pointing to VisuFlow, a separately distributed Eclipse-based debugging tool developed by the research group.

what: Providing configurable diagnostic output to support debugging, without breaking the output expected by command-line users.
why: Soot had no logging framework: all output went to a single PrintStream with ad-hoc verbosity guards. After the migration, mapping general messages to logger.debug and shipping no SLF4J backend left the command-line tool silent.
how: Added SLF4J loggers to every class using G.v().out, mapped messages to debug, warn and error levels, and deprecated G.v().out. The follow-up SOOT-916 reverted soot.Main to System.out/System.err to restore command-line output.

what: Supporting symbolic execution for path-constraint computation and input generation on top of the framework.
why: Symbolic execution is not part of Soot; it was developed only as a separate research effort whose code was withheld until publication and never released.
how: Unresolved. The student developer described the approach in a comment, but the code was never released or merged, and later status requests went unanswered. The issue remains open.

what: Communicating the status of announced but unreleased framework features to users.
why: Soot has no built-in symbolic execution, and the student implementation announced in SOOT-54 was withheld pending publication and never released, leaving users without a status update.
how: Unresolved. No maintainer answered the status question, and the issue remains open.

what: Accessing implementations of published analysis techniques built on the framework.
why: SnuggleBug exists only as an unreleased research prototype that was never made open source, and any remaining code would be outdated relative to current WALA.
how: Won't fix. The maintainer stated that the implementation is not available.

what: Building the framework from source with a reliable and documented build process.
why: The build script and settings template assumed a developer setup that a fresh checkout does not provide, such as a sibling JastAdd checkout, a Unix-only shell script, and wrong jar paths. Later failures were environment-dependent (Ant, Java certificate, missing bundled dependencies).
how: No code change. Maintainers suggested commenting out parts of build.xml and listed the required JastAdd projects; users shared command-line workarounds, and maintainers recommended nightly builds. The issue was closed for inactivity without fixing the build script.

what: Keeping the framework's build and runtime compatible with new JDK releases.
why: JDK 24 introduced a new class-file version and required a newer Gradle, and Temurin's JDK 24 builds ship without the .jmod files on which WALA's default standard-library loading relies.
how: Bumped the class-file version accepted by Shrike, added JDK 24 to CI, switched CI and the Gradle toolchain to a JDK distribution that includes .jmod files (Zulu/Azul), and updated Gradle and Guava.

what: Ensuring thread safety of shared framework data structures accessed during parallel processing.
why: Undetermined
how: Not merged. The maintainer rejected both proposed versions, stating that a real fix requires concurrent data structures. getMethodsByNameAndParamCount was later changed to use a ConcurrentHashMap, likely in SOOT-2214.

what: Delivering support for new language versions in official releases in a timely manner.
why: Support for Java 9+ had been developed on a separate branch but was not merged and released, partly due to limited maintainer resources, while the user could only use official releases.
how: Resolved by a later release: the maintainers merged the java9 branch and published Soot 4.0.0 with support for Java versions beyond 8.

what: Using the framework correctly when its APIs have evolved and older documentation or versions are still in use.
why: The user was working with an outdated WALA version and API: PolyglotJavaSourceAnalysisEngine had been removed, and source-level Java instructions must be handled by AstJavaModRef rather than the default ModRef visitor.
how: No code change. The maintainer pointed the user to AstJavaModRef in the latest WALA, and the reporter confirmed they had used the wrong version.

what: Reporting violations of IR invariants with informative error messages at the point where they occur.
why: The user's transformation used a new local without adding it to the body's local chain, violating an implicit invariant that was not checked on insertion. The violation surfaced only later as a bare NullPointerException.
how: Commit df80cdf extended UsesValidator to check that every used local is in the body's local chain, reporting a descriptive ValidationException at the offending unit instead of an NPE.

what: Providing clear diagnostics when framework setup or class loading fails.
why: Undetermined. Maintainers suspected infinite recursion but did not reproduce it; a misconfigured classpath likely explains the later 'can't find classfile' error, but not the silent termination.
how: No code change. Maintainers suggested debugging, alternative APIs and setting a process directory, but the reporter still failed. The issue remains open.

what: Keeping test configurations consistent with the project structure as test resources are reorganized.
why: The Eclipse JUnit launcher's classpath pointed to examples-src in the test project instead of the separate test-data project, likely because the launch file was not updated when test data was moved.
how: Corrected the classpath entry in the launch file to point to the test-data project.

what: Keeping API documentation accessible and links stable as project hosting and websites change.
why: The website redesign dropped the link to the browseable API docs, the build published JavaDoc only as a download, and later server moves broke old links without redirects.
how: The build was changed to publish browseable JavaDoc, and maintainers provided updated links as hosting moved. Some old links remain broken.

what: Keeping getting-started documentation and examples up to date so new users can run the framework.
why: The Getting Started instructions were outdated and did not explain that the build places JLex.jar automatically, and JavaScript call-graph construction was documented only on the old SourceForge wiki.
how: Updated the Getting Started wiki page, pointed to the JavaScript front-end documentation, and added a JavaScript call-graph example to the WALA-start repository. No change to the WALA codebase.

what: Governing repository access and project infrastructure for a widely used open-source framework.
why: Soot was hosted under a shared lab organization whose owners all implicitly had write access, so access control could not be scoped to Soot, and the build depended on the group's own Jenkins infrastructure.
how: Moved Soot to a dedicated soot-oss organization with a new Maven group id, replaced Jenkins with GitHub Actions, and updated links. The issue remains open, with wiki URL updates, JavaDoc hosting and related projects still pending.

what: Hosting project websites, downloads and documentation on trustworthy platforms.
why: SourceForge appeared to engage in questionable practices, so keeping the project site and downloads there was seen as a risk.
how: Partially done. A contributor ported the SourceForge user guide to the GitHub wiki, but completion of the migration is not recorded, and the issue remains open.
